name: Subhuman / LTN / HTN / Chad tiers

image.caption: L2370111 Człekokształtny moins qu'humain Subhuman infrahumano unmenschlich

lead: Tier language ranks men by perceived looks. The bottom is 'subhuman', the middle splits into low-tier normie (LTN) and high-tier normie (HTN), and the top is Chad, with further steps like giga Chad. It gives looksmaxxers a shared scale for setting a target tier and picking steps to climb.

The system descends from the PSL scale, which scores facial attractiveness from 1 to 8 and is built around assumptions about how women perceive men. Other descriptions use three tiers: subhuman, normie and Chad. The labels are informal community ratings rather than validated measures.

paras: Members rate faces against the scale, often in forum photo threads, and use the result to choose what to work on, from skin and grooming to fitness and procedures.
Critics note the labels can be dehumanising, and researchers consider parts of the PSL system pseudoscientific. Effects on self-image have not been formally studied in the sources reviewed.

chain: Rate faces on a tier scale
angle.text: Looksmaxxing and incel communities use these tiers, descended from the PSL scale, to rank men's attractiveness and to set a target tier to climb toward through improvements. The labels are informal community ratings rather than validated measures.

lead: Subhuman, LTN (low-tier normie), MTN (mid-tier normie), HTN (high-tier normie), Chadlite, Chad and giga Chad are the rungs of a tier vocabulary used in looksmaxxing communities to place a man's looks on a ladder. For the people who use it, the point of the ladder is orientation: knowing roughly where one's face sits suggests how far there is to go and which improvements, such as skin, body fat, grooming, hair or facial structure, might move someone up a step.[1][2]

The tiers descend from the PSL scale, a numeric rating of facial attractiveness whose name is commonly expanded as the three forums credited with creating it: PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.[1][2][3] Wikipedia describes the scale as running from 1 to 8 and as designed around how its authors believed women perceive men; community guides circulate several different numeric mappings, so there is no single standard.[1][2][4] A simpler three-step version associated with the streamer Clavicular sorts men into subhuman, normie and Chad.[1]

Researchers have studied the system mainly as a social phenomenon. Solea and Sugiura (2025) describe the PSL scale as a pseudoscientific framework that repackages incel ideology as self-improvement, and Halpin and colleagues (2025) analysed how a large looksmaxxing forum's rating culture shapes its members' health.[5][6] No study has tested the tiers as a validated measure of attractiveness.

paras: Subhuman (also sub-3 or sub-5 in some guides) is the lowest band. Low-tier, mid-tier and high-tier normie cover the middle of the range, where the community says most people fall, and Chadlite, Chad and giga Chad describe progressively more attractive men.[1][2] Know Your Meme's summary of the scale lists further sub-steps within each band (for example 'MTN+') and, above Chad, an Adam tier, with the top step described as largely unattainable.[2] Female counterparts include the Becky tiers (normie) and Stacy or Stacylite.[7][2]

The numeric mapping differs between sources. One Know Your Meme entry places HTN at 6 out of 10, between mid-tier normie (5) and Chadlite (7), with LTN at 4 and Chad at 8; another summary gives the band for HTN as 5.1 to 5.9 and Chad as 6.9 to 7.4 on a scale that reaches 7.9.[2][4] A third description reports that the community considers roughly 1.9 to 5.9 the range where most people fall.[3] The sources agree that the cut-offs are informal and that scores are assigned by community consensus rather than measured.[2][3]

Members often attach a tier word to the specifics of a face, so a single post may mention 'HTN' alongside comments on the eyes, jaw or skin.[8] Related vocabulary includes sexual market value (SMV), mogging (outshining another person's appearance), and the softmaxxing / hardmaxxing split between non-invasive and invasive improvement.[1]

Chad itself has an older history. The word was used in Chicago in the 2000s as a mildly derogatory term for a wealthy young man from the city's northern neighbourhoods, and a satirical website covered the fictional Lincoln Park Chad Society.[7] Incel forums of the 2010s adopted it for a sexually active, supposedly genetically advantaged man, and the 'Chad Thundercock' meme went viral on 4chan around 2013.[7] The 'Virgin vs. Chad' format appeared in 2017 and the 'Gigachad' image meme dates to 2016, built on black-and-white photographs of a muscular model from a photographer's art project.[7]

Looksmaxxing took shape on incel and manosphere message boards in the 2010s, where discussion credited sexual success to the genetic advantages of 'Chads'.[1] The rating vocabulary came out of three forums, PUAHate.com, Sluthate.com and Lookism.net, collectively called the PSL community. They are now defunct, but much of the terminology originated there.[1] Know Your Meme describes the scale as an attempt to give attractiveness an 'objective' number using geometric criteria, and notes that PSL is sometimes expanded as 'Proportion, Size and Lineation'.[2][3]

On looksmax.org, the abbreviation HTN is tagged to 2019 in Know Your Meme's entry, which cites a forum user rating someone as HTN as the earliest known use it could find. The entry then tracks guides to the scale appearing in September and December 2023, a thread on X in January 2024, and a June 2024 Reddit explainer.[4]

The vocabulary reached wider audiences in the early 2020s through TikTok, where early content was often framed as self-improvement with self-deprecating humour.[1] Videos that score faces on the scale, or parody its granularity with labels like 'LTN', 'MTN+' and 'HTN', became a recurring format, and Know Your Meme describes ironic 'slang overload' memes using the terms by early 2026.[2][4][3] Wikipedia lists coverage in Vice (2018), Business Insider and The New York Times (November 2023), The Conversation (January 2024), The Guardian and the BBC (2024), and, in 2026, profiles of the streamer Clavicular and a critique by Becca Rothfeld in The New Yorker.[1]

Clavicular, a Kick livestreamer, is cited as a major driver of the terms' mainstream reach.[1][2] In a July 2026 interview with Sean Hannity reported by Fox News, he described looksmaxxing as 'the most well-rounded form of self-improvement', and argued that appearance affects 'every single micro interaction in your life'.[9]

Solea and Sugiura, of the University of Portsmouth, published 'Digital subcultural diffusion theory: rebranding the incel ideology through Looksmaxxing, Sub5s and the PSL scale' in Crime, Media, Culture (online 16 November 2025). Drawing on TikTok, looksmax.org and Incels.Wiki, they argue that the PSL scale is a pseudoscientific construct whose scientific framing lends credibility to misogynist and racist views, and they call for better platform governance.[6] Know Your Meme quotes the same authors calling it a systematic pseudoscientific framework that codifies the incel hierarchical worldview.[2]

Halpin and colleagues' 2025 paper in Sociology of Health & Illness, 'When Help Is Harm', qualitatively analysed 8,072 comments from two boards of a looksmaxxing forum with about 6 million monthly visitors: one for self-improvement and one for user-submitted ratings. They report that members rank men on the PSL scale, which the community presents as objective; that white men rated 9 or 10 out of 10 are called Chads; that men around 5 are 'normies'; and that men rated 3 or lower are called 'subhuman'. The authors argue that this hierarchy applies a 'hegemonic masculine gaze' to men's bodies, pushes members toward medical and surgical self-alteration, and produces 'masculine demoralisation'. They note that the data is self-reported and unverified and that photos were not analysed.[5]

Wikipedia reports that critics call the practice judgemental and link it to body dysmorphia, and that Rothfeld's March 2026 New Yorker piece criticised the 'subhuman' label and racist language used by some participants.[1] The American Academy of Dermatology's page on looksmaxxing flags risks to body image and self-esteem, especially in adolescents, notes overlap with body dysmorphic disorder, anxiety and depression, and advises dermatologists to watch for disproportionate distress about minor findings.[10]

Critics quoted by Know Your Meme add two further objections: that beauty is subjective and cannot be reduced to geometric formulas, and that successful public figures with features the scale would count as flaws remain widely seen as attractive.[2][3] Some participants, by contrast, say the numeric vocabulary gives them a concrete way to talk about appearance; Wikipedia notes peer affirmation is reported alongside the critique.[1]

On looksmax.org the tier words appear in thread titles, rating requests and replies. Threads comparing a user's photos over time, such as one titled around moving from the lowest tier to low mid tier between ages eleven and thirteen, show the vocabulary applied to change through puberty; some replies respond that the change was simply growing up, so members themselves question what a tier movement means.[8]

Because the tiers are tied to the face, forum members typically discuss specific traits such as skin, leanness, eye area and jaw when explaining a rating, and treat these as the levers for moving up.[1][5][8] Photo-rating boards are the main setting for this, and Halpin and colleagues describe them as a place where ratings are tied to suggestions for interventions.[5]
The terms have also appeared beyond forums. In 2025 a Hacker News thread discussed a chatbot reported to recommend extreme surgeries to men it labelled 'subhuman'.[11]

Tier talk sits alongside softmaxxing (skincare, grooming, clothing, fitness, and practices such as mewing) and hardmaxxing (off-label drugs, dieting, cosmetic surgery and similar invasive steps), as described by Wikipedia.[1] The AAD's page on looksmaxxing groups orthodontic care, cosmetic surgery and unregulated interventions under 'hardmaxxing' and lists dermatologic complications associated with at-home and experimental practices.[10]

No studies found. Related social-science research is described above: qualitative and media analyses of the PSL scale and looksmaxxing forums, not trials or validation studies of the tier system.[5][6]

lore.intro: Members use tier labels in photo-rating threads, in discussions of what holds a given face back, and in jokes about the scale's own granularity.[4][8]
